rows.title: With Telluride resort closed amid ski patroller strike, visitation drops as nearby resorts salvage holiday ski vacations
rows.standfirst: Patrollers say Telluride Ski and Golf has not reached out to resume contract negotiations as the resort makes snow and promises “a safe re-opening as soon as possible.”

rows.title: Fort Morgan’s “Home Town Takeover” was anything but perfect. But nearly 3 years on, it’s still reaping the benefits.
rows.standfirst: Town Manager Brent Nation said the community of 12,000 didn’t know it had beaten out 5,000 applicants until “Hollywood” showed up with NDAs and demands on the local government

rows.title: What’s Working: Colorado’s retirement program sees 38% growth in savers
rows.standfirst: Most of the state’s employers, however, haven’t joined SecureSavings. Officials cleaned out 33,000 records of bad employer data and expect to start enforcement this year. Plus: Minimum wage updates, paid-family leave changes and new labor laws.

rows.title: 14 things that will make headlines in Colorado in 2026
rows.standfirst: From wolves and water to Medicaid and midterms, The Colorado Sun’s newsroom looks ahead to what we’ll be watching this year

rows.title: A private water company is leading a $150 million rush for northern Colorado groundwater
rows.standfirst: The fast moving Front Range H2O hopes to deliver its first water to the Fort Collins-Loveland Water District by early 2029

rows.title: Education funding chaos weighs on Colorado community and rural colleges
rows.standfirst: Cuts to programs perceived as having a DEI focus are hitting training for nurses, cops, welders and other high-skill trades hard

rows.title: Telluride ski patrol union approves a new contract, ending strike and preparing resort re-opening this weekend
rows.standfirst: The ski patrol accepted less than what they wanted as pressure from struggling businesses and workers mounted

rows.title: Colorado professional jobs saw large decline in November, but signs of hope appear for tech workers
rows.standfirst: The professional and business services sector lost 1,200 jobs in November. But inside that sector, tech jobs see improvement.

rows.title: Colorado Democrats, labor movement revive push to ease unionization rules. Jared Polis is promising another veto.
rows.standfirst: Democrats took a stab at the policy during last year’s legislative session and worked for months to find a compromise between unions, business groups and the governor’s office. But the negotiations fell apart.

rows.title: What’s Working: A couple of friends thought they could help build affordable housing in Pagosa Springs. Was it wishful thinking?
rows.standfirst: The project has been stymied by infrastructure, utility costs and some community pushback. Plus: Colorado jobs, junk fees, bioengineered food labels and more!

rows.title: A rural Colorado hospital, amid constant funding struggles, draws lifeblood by leveraging lab services
rows.standfirst: Keefe Memorial, a critical access hospital in Cheyenne Wells, has partnered with a company to bring innovation to longstanding economic challenges

rows.title: When a landlord ghosted its Denver tenants, trash and dog poop piled up. Then came the mysterious fees.
rows.standfirst: Colorado lawmakers have steadily expanded protections for tenants in recent years, but many renters still find it hard to reason with out-of-state investment firms.

rows.title: Colorado Springs seeks bill to keep Ray Nixon coal plant open past 2029 closure deadline
rows.standfirst: After a reprieve last week from Trump’s EPA, Colorado Springs utilities now wants an exemption by the state government

rows.title: Greeley will vote on the biggest development project in town history. Here’s why the $800 million plan is contentious.
rows.standfirst: A new arena for the Colorado Eagles, an entertainment district and future housing are all part of the plan, which opponents say Greeley cannot afford

rows.title: Realtors say it’s still a buyer’s market in Colorado, but high housing costs keep renters renting
rows.standfirst: The market continues to get worse when it comes to condos and townhouses, with rising homeowner fees a major factor

rows.title: The big bills to watch as Colorado’s 2026 legislative session begins
rows.standfirst: Colorado lawmakers open their lawmaking term trying to tackle big issues — like housing, the environment and public safety — under a strained budget

rows.title: Bargain grocer Aldi seizes the moment by expanding into Colorado in an era of higher prices
rows.standfirst: The company is also looking to open more than 50 stores in Colorado within the next five years

rows.title: Colorado PUC moves to give extra financial help to towns losing coal-fired power plants, but there’s a catch
rows.standfirst: The plants must shut down as planned, which is complicated by Trump administration actions to bolster the coal industry

rows.title: What’s Working: The fees Colorado consumers still face after “junk fee” law has taken effect
rows.standfirst: It wasn’t a law to get rid of fees, only to bring attention to them before the bill arrives. Here are other fees that must be disclosed by state and federal policies.

rows.title: Colorado governor asks FEMA to reverse rejection of $41M in disaster aid after Western Slope floods, fires
rows.standfirst: Polis adds an official appeal to the voices of elected officials, including U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd, who worry about the economic consequences of the natural disasters

rows.title: Arkansas Valley pipeline has about 3 years of cash left to keep building, despite presidential veto
rows.standfirst: But local and state officials say without more help from the feds, the project to bring safe drinking water to southeastern Colorado will be halted again

rows.title: Tariffs keep Colorado’s small businesses guessing, as state’s exports increase but imports fall
rows.standfirst: Trade with the state’s top three partners fell in the first 10 months of 2025, with Chinese imports dropping 25%.

rows.title: Apartment vacancy in metro Denver reaches highest rate in 16 years, pushing down rents again
rows.standfirst: Fourth quarter 2025 also saw landlords offering more free rent, gift cards and other concessions than in apartment industry report’s 21-year history

rows.title: Downtown Denver’s office vacancy rate grows to 38.2% as tenants reimagine the workplace
rows.standfirst: Much of the downtown submarkets ended 2025 more than 40% empty. But as available sublease space diminishes, the industry hopes stabilization is afoot.

rows.title: Your Xcel Energy bill is already going up amid Colorado’s current winter storm. Here’s why.
rows.standfirst: Wholesale natural gas is spiking, and you could pay up to a dollar more a month just for this weekend cold spell

rows.title: What’s Working: So many new Colorado businesses filed to start up in 2025, but renewals declined
rows.standfirst: Fourth-quarter business filings results are in, as are other year-end reports. Plus: apartment rent incentives, municipal budgets and more.

rows.title: Surveillance, captive-audience and wholesale pricing are in Colorado Democrats’ cost-of-living crosshairs
rows.standfirst: Many business groups are already lobbying against the measures. Gov. Jared Polis, as well as more moderate Democrats at the Capitol, could pose a roadblock to the bills becoming law, too.

rows.title: Longtime festivalgoers say the final Sundance in Utah may also be their last
rows.standfirst: The festival is moving to Colorado starting next year

rows.title: Colorado women earn 81 cents on every dollar earned by men, and child care costs are making it worse
rows.standfirst: National and state women’s advocacy groups are calling for changes in child care, job discrimination, maternal health care

rows.title: Colorado now has 6 million people, even amid slowing population growth
rows.standfirst: But the state saw more folks move out of state than move in. The State Demography Office attributes the declines in net migration to migrants who left.

rows.title: State regulators get an earful on Xcel power shutdowns from Coloradans left without electricity for days
rows.standfirst: State utilities regulators collected testimony from 4,000 businesses, households with lifesaving medical equipment and the merely annoyed as they form rules for public safety power shut-offs

rows.title: This 73-year-old Puebloan fixes planes for clients like a Saudi prince. Become an airplane mechanic and write your own ticket too.
rows.standfirst: Aviation-related jobs are in high demand. Plus: Colorado unemployment rate falls to 3.8%, state adds 23,000 jobs last year and updates from Colorado Springs.
